title: Shooting victim 'longed for family'
article: A man shot a dozen times by two junior Vancouver police constables in 2004 was looking forward to being reconnected with his 14 siblings once he got out of prison, a coroner's inquest was told Tuesday.

The statement was made by Sam Beaton, who was Gerald Chenery's parole office at Mission prison, where Chenery was serving a sentence for robbery until he was released three days before he was fatally shot.
Beaton recalled Chenery wanted to be reunited with his family in the Queen Charlottes when he was released from prison.
Officials, however, rejected Chenery's request because one of the conditions of his release was that he live under the supervision of a residential facility -- a halfway house.
"We don't have halfway houses up in that area," Beaton told a five-woman jury and presiding coroner Stephen Fonseca, who are probing the events that led to the fatal police shooting.

Instead, Chenery was released to a Vancouver halfway house, where he didn't know anyone, on Dec. 23, 2004. He had served 18 months of his 28-month sentence for robbing the Virgin Records store in Vancouver five times.
Chenery's prison file made him sound like a violent person, Beaton recalled, but the offender was friendly, pleasant to deal with and generally happy and optimistic.
"I never had a problem with him," Beaton testified. "He said he had been frustrated and angry with the way things had gone and his life in general."
But after getting a day pass from prison to attend his mother's funeral in August 2004, Chenery was reunited with his 14 siblings and his father, and his mood seemed more upbeat.
"It was quite a heart-warming family reunion," said Beaton, an employee of the Correctional Service of Canada. "Things seemed to change for him when his mother passed away."

Chenery's prison release was set for Dec. 27, 2004 but he was released early because of the Christmas holidays, so officials had to scramble to find a halfway house that met his needs, Beaton testified.
The witness said Chenery's death, days after his release "troubled me for quite some time afterwards . . . the fact things turned out so abysmally."
Chenery, who had a history of crack cocaine abuse, encountered two Vancouver police officers on a routine patrol on Hastings Street on Dec. 26, 2004.
Police said shortly after the fatal shooting that Chenery began walking away as soon as he saw the officers, which caused them to stop their patrol car to investigate.

When the officers, a man and a woman, asked Chenery if he was armed, Chenery pulled a serrated steak knife. The officers demanded Chenery drop the knife. Instead, he pulled a second knife and charged at the female officer, who fired four shots, one of which hit Chenery.

When the shot failed to stop Chenery, the male officer fired 11 shots from his semi-automatic Beretta pistol, hitting Chenery in his back, wrists and leg. The officers are expected to testify today at the inquest.

Chenery's older sister, Theresa, 31, testified her brother's death was so devastating for her that she lost custody of her five children. "I fell apart after he died," she said outside coroner's court.

She and her siblings had been born in Prince Rupert and grew up in an abusive home with parents who drank heavily. The native Indian kids were placed in different foster homes with white families, she said, adding her parents had been victims of the native residential school system.
She said Gerald was placed in a foster home with an RCMP officer in Prince Rupert who would put Gerald in a jail cell for punishment.
"The system that tried to save us from abuse put us in foster homes that were not safe," she said. "It really caused us more tragedy in our lives that was not necessary."
Another sister, Edith Fee, 28, said outside court that she expected her brother to be released from prison after Christmas.
Her older sister, Sylvia Fee, added: "We all held it in our hearts that we were going to be together again."
